threads_text: A tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, version 2.1.313, sat in Cursor's marketplace for about 11 hours and reached up to 5,000 users. It quietly added an attacker's SSH key and survived being uninstalled. Do you check your editor extensions before they auto update?

site_article.seo_title: Claude Code extension 2.1.313 backdoor hit up to 5,000 Cursor users
site_article.seo_description: A tampered Claude Code extension, version 2.1.313, added an attacker SSH key and a reverse tunnel. What happened and what affected developers should do.
site_article.answer_summary: Version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension, distributed through Cursor's marketplace on October 29, 2026, contained a backdoor that Anthropic did not write. Users who installed it should remove persistence files, check their SSH keys, install 2.1.314 or later and rotate credentials.

paragraphs.text: A modified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension for VS Code, listed as version 2.1.313, reached the extension marketplace used by the Cursor code editor on October 29, 2026, and carried hidden code that opened a backdoor on developer machines. Cursor said at most 5,000 of its users received the build, and that the version was not developed by Anthropic.

According to a timeline published by the security firm StepSecurity, the tampered build went live at about 09:27 UTC on October 29, which Cursor gave as 2:27 a.m. Pacific Time. Cursor removed the version at 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time the same day and took its marketplace fully offline, leaving an exposure window of roughly 11 hours. A clean version, 2.1.314, was published early on October 30.

Cyber Press, citing an analysis by the researcher Paul McCarty and the security project OpenSourceMalware, reported that the attackers prepended a 66-line function to the extension's main JavaScript file while leaving the rest of the package identical to the real release. The code ran as soon as the extension module loaded, so it did not need a user to start a conversation with Claude.

Both StepSecurity and Cyber Press said the code added an attacker-controlled SSH key labeled svc-telemetry to the user's authorized keys file and tried to switch on remote login. It then opened a reverse SSH tunnel to a server at 134.209.82.225 and sent unencrypted reports with the host name, user name, operating system and the names of environment variables that looked like passwords, tokens or cloud keys. Cyber Press reported that the values of those variables were not included in the first report.

The code also installed ways to restart itself: a LaunchAgent on macOS, a scheduled task called SysMon on Windows and a startup entry in cron on Linux. StepSecurity warned that uninstalling the extension alone is not enough, because these pieces keep running on their own.

The reports differ on the path the build took. StepSecurity said it appeared on Open VSX, the open extension registry, and reached Cursor through the mirror Cursor syncs from it, under the legitimate Anthropic publisher name. Cyber Press reported that Cursor confirmed the compromise started in its own marketplace rather than in Open VSX. Tech Insider noted that it is still not known who modified the extension or how many machines actually ran the code.

Cursor said no other extensions were tampered with, rotated its keys and published cleanup scripts for macOS and Windows. According to StepSecurity, Cursor also said the attacker's server was taken offline with help from its hosting provider.

StepSecurity advised anyone who had version 2.1.313 installed to look for the svc-telemetry entry in their SSH authorized keys, save evidence and remove the restart files, then install 2.1.314 or later. It also recommended rotating every credential the machine could reach, including source control, cloud, CI and package registry tokens, preferably from a different, clean computer, and rebuilding the machine if the tunnel ever connected. Tech Insider stressed that updating to 2.1.314 does not remove anything the bad build left behind.

The attack shows how much trust developers place in editor extensions. A coding assistant runs with the same access as the person using it, and a single tampered update was enough to give an outsider a door into machines that hold source code and cloud keys. The fact that the build looked like an official release under a familiar name made it harder to spot.

The next thing to watch is an explanation from Cursor, Open VSX or Anthropic of how the tampered build was published, and whether any machines that received it show signs that the attacker actually logged in.
